entries.title: Caps Lose 5-1 to Wild, Snapping Three-Game Win Streak
entries.summary: Justin Sourdif scored the only goal for Washington in the final moments of the second period.
entries.content:
Quinn Hughes and Michael McCarron scored in the first 5:27 for Minnesota, and the Wild held on for a 5-1 victory over the Washington Capitals on Sunday.

Justin Sourdif scored the only goal for Washington in the dying seconds of the second period, but the Capitals’ three-game winning streak came to an end during this visit by the Central Division-leading Wild.

Maxim Shabanov’s power-play goal with 2:23 left in the third restored a two-goal margin, and Kirill Kaprizov added an empty-netter for his 500th career point and league-leading 15th goal of the season.

With 24.9 seconds left and the goalie back in, Danila Yurov scored one more for Minnesota.

Washington had scored at least four goals in five of its previous six games, but the Capitals ran into a stingy Minnesota team and goalie Jesper Wallstedt. The Wild permitted two goals or fewer for the fifth time in six games.

Minnesota has points in eight of its last nine.

Hughes opened the scoring after only 3:42 with his fifth goal of the season. McCarron’s shot from the slot made it 2-0.

Sourdif deflected the puck past Wallstedt to cut the lead in half.

Alex Ovechkin has just one goal in his first 13 games in what he’s said will be his final NHL season. Cole Hutson found him on the doorstep with a pass early in the third period, but with the net open, the puck bounced off Ovechkin’s skate and he wasn’t able to control it.

Ovechkin later had a shot from the slot denied by Wallstedt. Alex Tuch stole the puck near the Minnesota net but was stopped by Wallstedt as well.

Jordan Kyrou had a six-game point streak snapped for Washington.

Up Next

Capitals: Host Dallas on Tuesday night.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: The Commanders Get Back on Track in a 27-10 Win Against the Eagles
entries.summary: Washington scored 27 unanswered points to earn a crucial divisional win on "Sunday Night Football."
entries.content:
It wasn’t pretty — at times it was downright ugly. But the Commanders did enough to earn a 27-10 win against the Eagles on Sunday night.

Trailing 10-0 in the first quarter, it looked like Washington was well on its way to another demoralizing loss in a season full of them. But the defense stepped up, holding Philadelphia scoreless for the final three quarters and giving the Commanders' offense time to find a rhythm.

"There is an energy that comes from adversity that can be constructive or it can be destructive — for us it was constructive," coach Dan Quinn said. "[We decided] we were going to go fight, we were going to go battle."

Without the services of defensive tackles Daron Payne (leg) and Javon Kinlaw (knee), Washington allowed points on two of the first three drives of the game but shut Philadelphia down the rest of the way. The Commanders sacked Eagles quarterback Tanner McKee, filling in for Jalen Hurts, four times and forced a fumble. Corner Rasul Douglas nabbed an interception late in the fourth quarter to ice the game.

The run defense — one of the team's few bright spots this season — limited Eagles rushers to 91 yards on 29 carries. Saquon Barkley finished with just 54 total yards.

"We're looking for all four [quarters]," Quinn said. "We're getting closer, but we're not there yet."

On offense, Jayden Daniels wasn't efficient through the air (16 of 29 for 217 yards) but he threw a touchdown and went another game without an interception. The run game was missing starter Bill Croskey-Merritt for a second straight contest, but still managed to rack up 135 yards. Rachaad White had 11 carries for 55 yards and Austin Ekeler finished with 8 carries for 36.

Rookie receiver Antonio Wlliams, who Quinn said would see a bigger role after the season-ending injury to Terry McLaurin, was a steadying presence for Washington with five receptions for 54 yards.

"At some point you just have to hold yourself accountable," Williams said of the team's turnaround after the first quarter. "It comes from within."

Treylon Burks had a 53-yard reception that set up a field goal late in the third quarter. He led all receivers with 81 yards on the night.

Drew Stevens kicked four field goals, including a 56-yarder late in the first quarter. Daniels connected with Stefon Diggs for an 8-yard touchdown in the second quarter that tied the game at 10. On Washington's final drive of the first half, Daniels took a hard hit and was slow to get to his feet, but he stayed in the game.

The win, Washington's first since Week 3, moves the team to 2-4-1 and third place in the NFC East. The Cowboys (3-5) lost to the Cardinals on Sunday afternoon, keeping the divisional race close behind the first-place Giants. Washington faces the Rams (4-4) next week at home.

entries.title: CNN Panelists Worry for Haley Stevens After ‘Painful’ Interview
entries.summary: Stevens appeared on the network Sunday night to explain her eleventh-hour decision to cross party lines to back Rogers over El-Sayed.
entries.content:
In what can only be described as a remarkable moment of television, Rep. Haley Stevens took to CNN late Sunday to explain her endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers — but the interview quickly dissolved into a confrontational exchange that had the next guest stunned.

"This was one of the most painful interviews I've ever watched," said Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Michigan Democrat who said she has been concerned about Stevens for a week.

CNN’s Anderson Cooper made several attempts to nail down exactly what caused Stevens to switch her support from Abdul El-Sayed to Rogers since she had previously endorsed the Democratic nominee following her primary loss to him for the Senate seat from Michigan. But Stevens repeatedly deflected and referenced past scrutiny El-Sayed faced on the campaign trail — long before she was scheduled to appear with him on Sunday before her apparent, last-minute change in allegiance.

“It sounds like you're upset with me too, Anderson,” Stevens said.

“No, I'm not,” Cooper replied. “You're not really answering any of my questions, so it's somewhat frustrating.”

Panelists, including Democratic strategists David Axelrod and Van Jones, raised concerns about her mental state after watching her struggle in the interview with Cooper.

“I thought that was very, very sad, and you know, Haley Stevens is obviously struggling, and I think trying to find her way through something that she hadn't fully thought through,” Axelrod said after the interview.

Stevens described her decision to endorse Rogers as simply “where [she] was” after reviewing things about El-Sayed’s campaign.

“This is just a weight off my shoulders,” Stevens said. “Abdul has been getting angrier and angrier. I was trying to help, and I endorsed him. That ad was very painful.”

The ad Stevens referenced was run by an outside group linking the high costs for American consumers to U.S. aid for Israel and appeared to be at the center of the political fallout between El-Sayed and Stevens.

Cooper also pressed Stevens on reports that much of her staff had quit Sunday, citing her decision to support Rogers, but Stevens attributed the mass exodus to the natural “transition” that happens during a member of Congress’ last few weeks in office.

“There's just a couple weeks of lame duck left here,” Stevens said. “These are great individuals who I care a lot about, and certainly, they're free to share their views on this. I am not trying to upset anyone.”

Stevens told Cooper she had heard positively from other Democrats since switching her endorsement, but Dingell said Steven’s decision left many people “really stunned.” Dingell also confirmed that Stevens told her multiple times that she did not plan to endorse Rogers, but noted that she was “worried about her all last week.”

“She's a human being,” Dingell added. “I've had multiple conversations with her. I'm far from being the only one that has, and I'm very concerned that this has all become a distraction.”

El-Sayed said earlier that he was focused on more important things than Stevens’ change of heart.

“This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from the government,” El-Sayed told reporters outside of Northend Church of God in Christ in Detroit. “I’m a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about.”

President Donald Trump celebrated Stevens' endorsement during his rally in Iowa on Sunday, calling the Democratic congresswoman “brave” for breaking party lines to back the Republican.

“I'd love her to join the Republican Party,” Trump said. “Actually, I think that could happen maybe. But she showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the great people of Michigan, and that's another important election for us.”

When Cooper asked Stevens about her reaction to hearing the strong words of support from Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana), the Democratic congresswoman noted that that she voted to impeach the president twice and took a dig at Johnson by saying that “he's not been up to all too much.”
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Resigned to Political Drama
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 2, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: D.C. council intrigue, chaos at the District’s only public Montessori school and the Commanders in primetime.

Capital Weather's daily digit — 7/10: Once we shake a cool and cloudy start, we can look forward to a delightfully sunny and mild afternoon. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

At-Large council member Robert White will walk out of the Wilson Building for the last time later today, but he’s leaving plenty of political drama in his wake.

Who will succeed him — and who gets to pick — are questions that are being hotly contested, and this week could see plenty of jockeying and possibly legal action.

All of this started late last month, when White was forced to announce his resignation from the council after it became clear that a little-noticed provision of city law could imperil his ascension to the role of D.C.’s delegate to Congress unless he surrendered his council seat before Tuesday’s election.

Under normal circumstances, the job of picking an interim council member to fill his seat until a special election would be left to the D.C. Democratic Party. But rumors that At-Large colleague Christina Henderson, who is an independent, would change her party affiliation to Democrat raised the prospect that the Democratic Party could suddenly be muscled out of that process.

Democrats aren’t taking that possibility kindly. In a statement issued Friday afternoon, party leaders didn’t directly name Henderson, but they sent her a clear message regardless: “We are aware of efforts to go around the Party’s process. We know who is involved. To them, we say plainly: stop. There is one path to this seat, and it runs through the D.C. Democratic Party.”

At least two lawmakers have jumped in behind the Democratic Party: Ward 5’s Zachary Parker and Ward 8’s Trayon White, along with Shadow Senator Ankit Jain and former elections board chair Gary Thompson. Legally speaking, though, the issue is debatable and historically untested. If Henderson decided to push ahead, it could end up in court.

What’s Henderson saying? Nothing thus far, neither admitting nor denying whether she’s planning a party switcheroo. And regardless of what happens, D.C. voters will ultimately have a say in who finishes out White’s term in a special election likely to happen in the spring.

Still, the somewhat-insider brouhaha is of consequence to the D.C. Democratic Party, which doesn’t often get to play kingmaker-of-sorts for a council seat. And with a progressive faction having taken control of the party earlier this year, the stakes are higher still.





DEEP DIVE

Parents feel betrayed by a shift in curriculum at D.C.’s only public Montessori school, The Washington Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports.

Multiple parents said they signed their kids up for Capitol Hill Montessori at Logan for its avowedly Montessori approach, a unique curriculum under which teachers, often called “guides,” keep watch in the background of mixed-grade classrooms, and students learn practical life skills like gardening and baking.

But since a new principal took the helm over the summer, one without apparent experience with the Montessori curriculum, parents say there’s been a sudden shift. Citing assessment scores that were lower than the city average, instructional superintendent Gwendolyn Payton said the school would marry traditional public education with Montessori “philosophies.”

The change is causing some parents to look elsewhere for their children’s educations, and led to Ward 6 council member Charles Allen penning a letter to the interim chancellor of D.C. Public Schools to express his concerns.

“We built our community here,” one parent told The Sun, her voice breaking. “It makes me really sad that we potentially have to leave this because they've just destroyed it.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

Arch enemies: D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones are suing the Trump administration over President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch, The Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports, arguing it violates D.C.’s building height restrictions and poses environmental and safety threats both in the District and Virginia.

It’s the latest legal challenge to the arch. Another is a lawsuit filed in February by three Vietnam war veterans who argue the project sidestepped congressional approval and would impede the peaceful atmosphere of Arlington National Cemetery, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

D.C. should get control of more of the parkland in the city, says a new report from a local parks task force, noting that 90% of the current acreage is owned and operated by the National Park Service. The task force — led by former mayor Anthony Williams and Ward 3 council member Matt Frumin — argues that a city agency could better run parks that provide amenities for residents, writes The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle. To wit: There are 105 playgrounds on land operated by the D.C. Department of Parks and Recreation, but only 19 on land owned by NPS.

It’s all but certain that tomorrow, D.C. residents will vote Janeese Lewis George in as the District’s new mayor. City Cast D.C. reports that a local charitable foundation is already courting donors for a $2 million fund to ease that transition. In an interview with The Washington Post, the Democratic nominee detailed some of the issues she aims to take on early in her tenure, including a comprehensive housing plan that addresses rental nonpayment.

The Hirshhorn Sculpture Garden reopened this past weekend after a four-year-long renovation with nearly double the previous number of sculptures on display, Axios D.C. reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

A man has been hospitalized with life-threatening injuries after he accidentally fell onto the tracks at Virginia Square Metro station and was struck by a train Friday, WTOP reports.





HAPPY HALLOWEEN

D.C. goes hard for Halloween, and this year was no exception. One reader celebrated the 50-year anniversary of Stephen King’s “Carrie,” other Washingtonians poked fun at the effort to ban foie gras, but The Sun’s own Martin Austermuhle spotted what is perhaps the epitome of “D.C. Halloween” — these carved pumpkins:

https://x.com/maustermuhle/status/2116674027418722587?s=20



TRIVIA


Which D.C. mansion is said to be haunted by the ghost of Dolley Madison?

  1. Dumbarton House
  2. Decatur House
  3. The Octagon
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

Commanders 27, Eagles 10: Washington fans have reason for optimism this morning, not only because of a home win over the Eagles last night, but because the team is now a mere two games out of first place in the NFC East. After falling behind 10-0, the Commanders held the Eagles scoreless for three quarters and slowly built a lead. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson breaks down a crucial win.

The Spirit’s first-round playoff matchup is set. Washington will host Portland at 3 p.m. Sunday, after concluding the regular season with a 2-0 home win over Chicago yesterday. See the full NWSL playoff bracket here.

What to Watch Today:

NCAAW: Maryland vs. South Carolina, 12 p.m. (ESPN)

NBA: Wizards at Magic, 7:30 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jeff Dooley, Gaby Morera Di Núbila and Jaden Amos.

entries.title: Morning Sun: November Surprise
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The latest from the electoral map. An exclusive on Republican campaign spending after the Supreme Court ruled in favor of unlimited coordinated spending.

THE MAP


One day more: Donald Trump plans to deliver his closing message at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool today, after a long night rallying in Iowa and Kansas. Democrats’ closing argument seems to be reminding voters they are very good at disarray.

Michigan: Rep. Haley Stevens’ chaos agent turn. The Washington Sun’s Christa Dutton was in Detroit yesterday when the loser of the Democratic Senate primary formally endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens, who was initially going to appear at a rally yesterday with El-Sayed, had spent the previous few days accusing the Democrat of antisemitism for, as she put it, failing to adequately condemn an ad from an outside group. (El-Sayed’s campaign did condemn the ad.) Stevens supporters are apoplectic: Her official congressional staff resigned en masse, many of her Democratic colleagues want to kick her out of the caucus and allies are attacking her out of pure bewilderment. El-Sayed called it a “distraction.”

“Whole thing was really fucking bizarre,” a source familiar with Stevensworld told The Sun of Stevens and her fiancé, Jason Turkish, who endorsed Rogers days before Stevens did. “It is still unclear to me how he went from donor to fiancé.”

Stevens addressed the critics on CNN. “This is just a weight off my shoulders. Abdul has been getting angrier and angrier. I was trying to help, and I endorsed him. That ad was very painful.” Rep. Debbie Dingell, appearing on CNN right after, called that interview “painful.”

What we have here is a primary that never ended: The El-Sayed/Stevens race largely hinged on Stevens’ backing from AIPAC and her opponent’s strong support for Palestinians. It was a chasm Democrats remain for the most part unable to bridge. Democrats are used to being mad at lefties for refusing to get on the unity train (as recently as 2024 in Michigan, actually), and now they get to be mad at centrists.

That said, will it matter? The final New York Times/Sienna poll finds Democrats up in every Senate battleground race.

What’s next: For Democrats, a mad dash to use this as a unifying moment and get out the Election Day voter — even those living in Canada; Rebecca Ritzel reports for The Sun on a party effort to get hundreds of Americans living over the border to vote in Michigan. For Republicans, it’s a mad dash to take advantage of one of the more In Disarray moments Democrats have had in a long time.

More surprises across the map:

Alaska: DOJ Sullivan-gate lawsuit dismissed. A federal judge yesterday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. The DOJ immediately appealed to the 9th Circuit, which hasn’t been friendly so far to Trump administration efforts. “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” the DOJ posted on X.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) called the Democratic ballot confusion scheme “a stupid thing to do.”

Iowa: The skinny on Hinson getting skinny. In the first few minutes of Trump’s two-hour-long speech in Iowa yesterday, the president — who is quite vocal about what he thinks of others’ bodies — congratulated Rep. Ashley Hinson on her weight loss and claimed she did it “the old-fashioned way too, not with you know, give me a shot.”

“I knew Ashley for a long time, and she was a little bit heavier,” Trump said — adding that the Republican Senate candidate “knew the weight that was on her, really, literally the weight, and she knew the importance of what she was doing.”

Maine: Union split in final weekend. The Bangor Daily News reports on a familiar divide in the Senate race: The state council of the International Association of Machinists has endorsed Troy Jackson, while its Local S6 of Bath Iron Works has very publicly endorsed no one.

South Carolina: Regrets? Republicans have a few. “Privately, some Senate Republican campaign strategists and Trump advisers have grown alarmed about” Sen. Darline Graham, The Wall Street Journal reports. “Several said they believed they could have found a better candidate, but the president wanted Graham.”

Kansas: Roger Marshall goes off-script. The Republican senator posted a video responding to The New York Times’ story about lawsuits he filed against patients unable to pay medical debts owed to his OB-GYN practice, but Politico reports that his campaign “was not involved in creating” nor spent any money to promote it.

Ohio: The climate change election? “People don’t like paying more for energy,” Jed Ober, political director of NRDC Action Fund, told The Sun recently. It’s one of the reasons the spending arms of the Natural Resources Defense Council poured more than $20 million on ads against Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

Pennsylvania: Josh Shapiro’s 2028 audition. The Sun’s Alex Roarty spent time with the governor near the end of his foregone reelection campaign, in which he is also campaigning with Democratic House candidates. Shapiro is also using his pull to create the first Democratic trifecta in the state government since 1993. What does that add up to?

“There are a lot of people who are showing up because they’re scared about the direction our country’s heading in,” Shapiro told Alex, presidential-y, even as he brushed off speculation. “They’re angry about it. They want to do something to channel that anger, that fear, that concern, into action.”

Bonus: Shapiro on NBA GOATs: Alex asked the governor (and former basketball player) Shapiro who’s better, Michael Jordan or LeBron James, the latter of whom recently signed with the governor's hometown 76ers?

“LeBron's still playing. And so I think you’ve got to wait till his career is over,” the governor told Alex. “He has clearly surpassed Michael Jordan in terms of longevity. He is an incredible coach on the floor. Something I've been really impressed by, just watching him when he was on the floor or on the bench. I don't recall MJ having that similar type of approach on the floor. He was more kicking people’s butts around.”

More: California Is Testing the Appetite for a Wealth Tax • Abortion Opponents Warn Republicans That Ignoring the Issue Will Cost Them the Election • Justice Department Urges Sanctions for Analysis Critical of Its Noncitizen Voting Claims • A Super PAC Army Is Spending Millions on ‘Spoiler’ Candidates





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

First on The Sun: The NRCC’s nine-figure spending surge hit 60 House districts across the country this cycle after the Supreme Court opened the floodgates to unlimited coordinated spending. The Sun’s Alex Roarty got a first look at the NRCC’s final tally: $100 million to help Republicans hold onto their slim majority, even as most forecasters predict Democratic gains in the lower chamber Tuesday.

The Republican campaign arm fought all the way up to the high court in a yearslong legal battle to make this massive cash infusion possible, and Ryan Dollar, NRCC’s legal counsel, told Roarty they were ready to “put that victory to work immediately.”



More: Sen. Chris Murphy Hospitalized After a Stroke • Judge Throws Out Trump’s Suit Against the Wall Street Journal Over Epstein Letter • FBI Blames North Korea for Stolen Billions From Binance in Biggest Hack in History • Troops ‘Can’t Feel Genuinely Safe’ as Trump Weighs Iran Escalation





NOT US

  • An Arizona county was unprepared for the 2024 election. Navajo voters paid the price. By Sasha Hupka and Adriana Navarro for VoteBeat
  • Inside the Plan to Send 1,000 DOJ Monitors to the Polls, by Yvonne Wingett Sanchez, Madeleine Carlisle and Marie-Rose Sheinerman for The Atlantic
  • This Republican Wants Voters to Consider a Post-Trump World, by Jess Bidgood for The New York Times
  • Hegseth digs in as confident Democrats plan to go on offense after midterms, by Noah Robertson and Dan Lamothe for The Washington Post

entries.title: The NRCC Is Spending Over $100 Million on Coordinated Campaign Ads
entries.summary: The cash deluge is the product of a yearslong Republican effort to eliminate caps on coordinated spending.
entries.content:
House Republicans’ political arm is on track to spend more than $100 million on coordinated campaign ads by Election Day, according to an aide with the group — a surge of cash that has boosted GOP candidates as they try to hold their slim congressional majority.

The spending from the National Republican Congressional Committee — aided by a roughly $30 million contribution from the Republican National Committee — represents a large portion of the GOP’s overall advertising effort in House races this year. The cash flood has helped give Republicans a crucial spending edge over Democrats in many battleground districts.

“The NRCC built an advertising operation in cooperation with our partners to be the tip of the spear, providing early air support and putting a historic war chest to work across the battlefield in coordinated spending behind our candidates,” said Jack Pandol, the NRCC’s deputy executive director.

The spending went to 60 House districts, an NRCC official said.

The NRCC’s coordinated spending surge is the culmination of the committee’s effort to change how campaigns are funded and how that money can be spent, including for digital and TV ads.

In prior elections, groups like the NRCC faced significant limitations on how much cash they could legally spend in coordination with their candidates.

But a ruling from the Supreme Court this summer, in which the NRCC was a plaintiff, abolished coordination limits, allowing committees to spend freely on campaign ads from their own war chests.

That change was widely seen as a boon to Republican campaigns, in part because the RNC has an enormous cash-on-hand advantage compared to the Democratic National Committee.

“The NRCC proudly helped lead the legal effort in bringing the historic case that struck down unconstitutional limits on political parties supporting their own candidates,” said Ryan Dollar, NRCC’s legal counsel. “We were prepared to put that victory to work immediately, turning years of legal work into an operation that could deliver for our candidates when it mattered most.”

It remains to be seen whether the GOP’s financial edge will be enough to overcome a hostile political environment across the country. Most forecasters project that Democrats will win a House majority on Tuesday and, in recent weeks, Republicans have been forced to defend even some deep red seats.
entries.author: Alex Roarty

entries.title: California Is Testing the Appetite for a Wealth Tax
entries.summary: Voters will consider a ballot measure that would levy a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets.
entries.content:
Tuesday’s elections will be pivotal for the progressive movement to tax the rich.

Voters in California will decide whether to implement the nation’s first wealth tax, while three other states will consider ballot measures related to income tax rates for top earners.

If successful, these ballot measures could be a boon for the left’s push to raise taxes on the wealthiest Americans, potentially signalling that a federal wealth tax is a viable policy priority. Even if the measures fail, some advocates are claiming victory for getting the issue on the ballot at all.

“Obviously, we want this to pass, but already the economic credibility of the proposal, the political salience and the popular support for it already is a breakthrough,” said Nabil Ahmed, who is pushing for California’s Proposition 40 as the senior economic and racial justice director at Oxfam America. “It's also a vindication at the federal level that there's an economic credibility and a political salience to tax the richest people in this country.”

Proposition 40 would implement a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. Ninety percent of the revenue raised would fund health care, with the rest going toward education, food assistance and administering the tax itself.

But there are plenty of opponents — all the way up to Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom. The potential 2028 presidential candidate endorsed another ballot measure that would effectively ban the proposal.

“I’m voting no because this measure dedicates almost all of the revenue it raises to a single category of state spending,” Newsom wrote in a June Substack post about Proposition 40. “Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes. The fight belongs at the federal level, where this broken system was created in the first place.”

Many economists warn the measure could also drive wealthy taxpayers out of state, taking their tax dollars with them.

Billionaires have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into a campaign to defeat Proposition 40. At least six billionaires, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page and venture capitalist and Republican megadonor Peter Thiel, have said they moved out of the state because of the proposed wealth tax.

Even if billionaires don’t flee California en masse in the event of Proposition 40’s passage, economists said the measure could discourage business owners from moving there, depriving the state of new jobs and tax revenue.

“The risk is not just what happens to current taxpayers and do they leave and stop paying individual income taxes or shift their economic activity, but it's maybe even more so due to the next generation of founders that could drive California's economy,” said Jared Walczak, a senior fellow at the Tax Foundation.

The tax revenue losses could be more muted than expected, because California’s wealthiest have long weathered high taxes.

“It’s possible that those high-income, high-wealth taxpayers most inclined to leave when confronted with those high taxes [have] already left,” said Robert McClelland, a senior fellow at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center.

California voters also will consider a proposition to make permanent the state’s top marginal income tax rate of 10.3% to 12.3% on individuals earning more than $371,000. Revenue from the tax on those top earners helps fund schools and health care.

Three other states also have ballot measures seeking to change income tax rates on high earners.

North Carolina’s ballot includes a proposal to keep the maximum state income tax rate allowed by the state constitution at 3.5%.

Voters in Colorado will decide between two competing ballot measures — one to cap income taxes at the current rate of 4.4%, the other to establish a rate range of 3.7% to 8.4% to fund education and health care.

An initiative in Washington would repeal a state law placing a 9.9% tax on individual and household income over $1 million. The law is set to take effect in 2028 and would expand funding for schools, health services and a working families tax credit. Washington has no state income tax, but it does have a 6.5% sales tax.

Adam Glickman, secretary-treasurer of Service Employees International Union 775, noted that Washington’s current tax law translates to lower-income workers paying a higher portion of their earnings in sales tax.

Glickman said voters defending the income tax at the polls on Tuesday would send a message across the country that high taxes on the wealthy are politically viable.

“The lesson is that, one, people are willing to increase taxes to pay for critical public services, and two, that people do support increasing taxes particularly on the wealthy who have seen big gains in their income and wealth over the last decade,” he said.
entries.author: Jade Lozada

entries.title: Why Doesn’t D.C. Have More Control Over Its Parks?
entries.summary: In a new report, current and former city leaders argue that the National Park Service, which oversees 90% of parkland in D.C., should turn over more control.
entries.content:
D.C. has plenty of parks, but if you’re standing in one, there’s a good chance it isn’t owned or operated by the city’s government.

A new report from the D.C. Neighborhood Parks Task Force says that should change, and that the National Park Service should turn more of its parks and parcels over to local control.

“This continued federal control is a relic of the transition to Home Rule in the 1970s when the city had too much on its plate to worry about municipal parks management. Now the District has the capacity to do more,” former Mayor Anthony Williams wrote in an email to The Washington Sun. Williams co-chaired the task force with Ward 3 council member Matt Frumin.

While D.C. has 8,398 acres of parks, only 10% are actually controlled by the city, with the remainder falling under federal control by NPS. While some of those are established and historic destinations such as Meridian Hill Park or Lincoln Park, many of the parcels that NPS owns are actually small “pocket parks” in city neighborhoods that are of little federal interest and aren’t regularly tended to by NPS staff.

The report notes that federal parks tend to lack amenities for community residents. There are 105 playgrounds on land operated by the D.C. Department of Parks and Recreation, but only 19 on land owned by NPS. For basketball courts, the ratio is 122 local to 12 federal. As for dog parks and spray parks, virtually all of them are on D.C.’s land.

“Playgrounds, dog parks, movie nights, nature trails, accessible natural areas, and other common features of urban neighborhood parks are often not permitted on NPS-managed land. When uses are allowed, NPS must weigh any investments among competing needs within its budget,” the report says.

The challenges of the current land ownership situation are also felt by residents who may not know whether to call the District or NPS if they see something that needs to be fixed or addressed, or even snow that needs to be plowed in the winter. Some stretches of sidewalk and small traffic islands and circles are owned by NPS, which doesn’t have the same capacity to clear ice and snow that local agencies can have.

“The responsibility to manage the city’s local parks, reservations, and remnants is an unnecessary burden on NPS staff and resources,” the report says. “At the same time, the complex structure makes it challenging for the District government to provide the types of city parks and programming its residents and visitors need.”

City officials say the challenges with federal lands have been exacerbated by layoffs and job cuts over the past two years. Last year, Mayor Muriel Bowser wrote in a letter to the White House that “challenges persist on NPS properties where reduced staffing has impacted trash collection, graffiti removal, and overall maintenance.”

Still, the report notes that if D.C. were to gain more responsibility over parks and parcels currently owned by the federal government, the city would have to increase its own capacity to properly manage those lands. That could come by way of expanding DPR or creating a new coordinator of the public realm position modeled after a similar post in New York City.

The report also says D.C. should look to the NeighborSpace initiative in Chicago, a nonprofit land trust that works with community groups to maintain small parks and gardens, and consider new opportunities for raising more revenue from the parks the city currently controls. The report says D.C. recovers less than 5% of its parks and recreation costs; the national average is 26%.

Any effort to transfer more federal parks to D.C. would take a White House that is amenable to it. The Trump administration has shown particular interest in renovating certain federal parks in the city, but also was supportive of D.C. gaining more control over the RFK campus on the east end of Capitol Hill, which will be used for a new Commanders stadium and some 70 acres of parks.

There have been coordinated pushes over the years to either turn over federal land to D.C. or find creative solutions that allow the city to manage federal parks. That latter option is evident at Franklin Park in downtown D.C., where the city paid for a $21 million renovation after reaching an agreement with the federal government, and in Lincoln Park, where a nonprofit community group helps NPS with upkeep. There are also ongoing plans to transfer 110 acres of parkland at Poplar Point over to the city.

Williams, the former mayor, thinks the upcoming change in city leadership is a perfect opportunity to re-energize discussions around how to improve parks in the city.

“The city will have the first new mayor in over a decade. It’s an opportunity for real change in how the city embraces its parks,” he said.

entries.title: At D.C.’s Only Public Montessori School, Parents Are Feeling Betrayed
entries.summary: Tensions have risen at Capitol Hill Montessori at Logan since the school rolled out an amended curriculum that parents say is not what they signed up for.
entries.content:
It was the presence of glue sticks on the back-to-school list that caused Anita Thurakal to grow concerned.

Her son had been looking forward to another year at Capitol Hill Montessori at Logan, the only dedicated public Montessori institution in D.C., which typically relied on specific Montessori materials. So the unusually long back-to-school list, filled with crayons, pencils and other items traditionally found in a conventional classroom, made her take notice.

Thurakal and other parents’ concerns have only solidified in recent months, with a growing number expressing frustration at what they describe as a sudden shift in curriculum — one that is moving away from the Montessori model and more closely resembles a traditional public school.

Multiple parents told The Washington Sun that they feel both betrayed over the change in approach and powerless to stop it — and that after seeking out a Montessori education for their children, they’re only receiving a modified version, at best.

“We built our community here,” Thurakal told The Sun in an interview, her voice breaking. “It makes me really sad that we potentially have to leave this because they've just destroyed it.”

Tensions have begun to boil over, resulting in clashes between parents and the school’s new principal, with some parents handing out cautionary flyers at back-to-school night. Advocates have testified in front of the state board of education, and even D.C. Council members are raising concerns.

And, like Thurakal, several parents have said they may seek new schools for their children, possibly in the middle of this school year.

“I would have just never thought that they would do such an immense overhaul of what they were doing in previous years,” Thurakal said. “Because it had been working so beautifully.”

Technically, any school can call itself “Montessori,” because the name is not trademarked. But many schools seek accreditation from bodies like the American Montessori Society or the Association Montessori Internationale, the organization originally created by Dr. Maria Montessori. The Montessori approach is known for teachers, often called “guides,” keeping watch in the background of mixed-grade classrooms and students learning practical life skills like gardening and baking.

CHML has AMI certifications and AMI-trained teachers, and on its website, Capitol Hill says that its mission is built on the “100-year-old, evidence-based Montessori approach” — something parents cited as reason for wanting their kids to attend.
Capitol Hill Montessori at Logan (7008x4672, AR: 1.50)Much of the ire has been focused on Shelly Gray, who was hired as the school’s principal over the summer. Gray, who declined a request for comment, does not have experience with a Montessori curriculum listed on her DCPS biography page. She and other leadership officials, while not going so far as to say the school is abandoning its Montessori philosophy, have acknowledged some intention to change the school’s approach.

During a virtual September meeting between Gray, DCPS officials and parents, instructional superintendent Gwendolyn Payton addressed the issue.

“I want everyone to hear this as I speak for the team from the Office of Schools: There is no effort to dismantle, eliminate, reduce or diminish Montessori programming at Capitol Hill,” she told the 90-plus people who had tuned in.

But, Payton said, the school was making tweaks to its approach. Citing assessment scores that were lower than the city average (something parents pushed back against, given the differences in structure and grade levels between Montessori and other schools), Payton said that the way forward would involve marrying DCPS’s traditional curriculum with Montessori “philosophies.”

“We do not lower the rigor,” she repeated more than once while explaining the new system. “We increase the independence.”

Parents jumped into the meeting’s chat room, wanting to know why there was no prior communication about the changes. One said she and others felt “a sense of betrayal.”

Tensions only increased as the school year got going. On Oct. 1, almost a month after the meeting with Payton, a group of parents organizing under the name “Montessori Advocates of CHML” wrote a letter to Dr. Kim Jackson, the interim chancellor of D.C. Public Schools, arguing that “AMI accreditation is a demanding standard reserved for schools that adhere to the Montessori curriculum with fidelity, not a label DCPS can preserve informally while the conditions that earned it erode underneath.”

Many teachers found themselves caught up in the chaos, as well. Multiple parents told The Sun they feel bad asking teachers to act as liaisons with Gray, because in many cases the teachers themselves are not happy with the shift in curriculum.

“I know I really want to protect my teacher because there's a lot of tension between them,” said one parent who spoke on the condition of anonymity to protect the teacher’s identity. “[Gray is] really forcing hands against the Montessori-trained teachers who want to remain Montessori.”

The parent said that relationships among teachers, parents and Gray have become so strained that she only plans to keep her child in the school if Gray departs.

Earlier this month, Jackson told parents that Gray and Payton have been “working closely with District leadership and engaging directly with AMI to better understand Montessori accreditation requirements and ensure alignment.” AMI declined an interview request.

In a statement, a DCPS spokesperson told The Sun that “CHML and DCPS remain dedicated to the school continuing as an accredited Montessori program.” Acknowledging the changes to the primary level at CHML, or those serving students between the ages of 3 and 6, the spokesperson said, “There is still a robust period available for students to direct their own learning in uninterrupted work cycles of one to two hours each day. The intent of these adjustments is not to replace Montessori practices, but to strengthen instruction while preserving the core features that define the CHML experience.”

That deviation from the school’s previous approach is disappointing to parents like Marques and Asia Banks, who placed CHML at the top of their list in D.C.’s public school lottery after touring several Montessori schools last year and determining that the curriculum seemed perfect for their 3-year-old. Another plus: Just five years ago, DCPS put $61 million into renovating the school building near Union Square, making it better equipped for Montessori education with large, well-lit rooms and ample outdoor garden space.

The Bankses were convinced by the “long-standing traditions” at Capitol Hill and teachers who were “really grounded in the Montessori philosophy.” They submitted one of nearly 700 pre-K 3 applications for the 2026-27 school year.

But just two weeks into this school year, their son’s pre-K schedule seemed off. There didn’t seem to be the traditional three-hour, self-led block of time. After the couple joined the parent group chat, their fears were validated.

“Our child is young … and this is our first foray into this,” Asia said. “A 3-year-old cannot come home and tell us that there are changes to our expectations.”
Capitol Hill Montessori at Logan (7008x4672, AR: 1.50)The change in expectations is causing some parents to look elsewhere. Midyear D.C. school lottery applications are already open for parents who wish to move before the year is out. Applications for next school year will open in mid-December.

“We're going into the lottery, and I think there's a lot of parents who are doing this,” said one parent. “The curriculum has changed so dramatically. Some teachers I know are trying their best to hold on to some of the Montessori work, but because of the schedule changes, it's just not possible.”

City officials have begun to take action. Ward 6 council member Charles Allen recently wrote a letter to Jackson, expressing concern over changes at the school.

“I am concerned these actions are significantly harming the ability to deliver the educational method embedded in the name and identity of the school itself, as well as a method that parents, families, students, and educators affirmatively choose in becoming a part of this school community,” Allen wrote.

Thurakal is still considering how to move forward. Public Montessori schools near the District are limited, and she believes her son has surpassed grade-level expectations for traditional schools.

“This is what I want for him,” she said. “This is how I want him to grow up. Like I just feel so cheated for [the students].”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Football Players of Week 10
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts include a senior leader from Maret and a speedy sophomore from Langley.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

Last week marked the conclusion of the regular season high school football in the D.C. area. With the arrival of the postseason, here are five locals who earned All-DMV player of the week honors:

Hunter Humphries, Senior, Quarterback, Churchill

In a tough county matchup against Paint Branch last week, the Bulldogs relied on their senior leader to end the regular season on a high note. Humphries pieced together an efficient performance, completing 19 of his 22 passes for 204 yards and throwing two touchdowns. He also added a third score on the ground as Churchill pulled out a 28-13 win over the Panthers.

“We put so much on [Humphries] and we rely on him so much,” Churchill coach Joe Rydzewski said. “But in big situations, there’s nobody else I’d rather have with the ball in their hands.”

Trysten Johnson, Senior, Quarterback, Maret

This year’s Maret team is the youngest squad that coach Mike Engelberg has coached in his 21 seasons with the Northwest D.C. program. Of its 22 starters, 12 are freshmen or sophomores. Despite their youth, the Frogs picked up a statement 36-22 victory over St. Albans on Friday to move to 7-1 on the year.

Much of that success is thanks to Johnson, one of the team's few veterans. The dual-threat senior, committed to The Citadel, rushed for 174 yards and two touchdowns and added 116 passing yards and three more scores in Friday’s victory.

“If we are in the wrong protection and someone comes through untouched, [Johnson] goes up, he talks to them, he calms them down and we fix it,” Engelberg said. “The leadership he’s providing in the sense of his positivity goes a long way.”

Aiden Mejia, Sophomore, Athlete, Langley

Just a sophomore, Mejia has already made a name for himself as one of the most explosive athletes in Northern Virginia. The underclassman, who rotates between wide receiver and running back, has catalyzed another strong offensive season for the Saxons, who picked up a 21-7 win over Marshall on Friday.

Mejia accounted for 186 total yards and two touchdowns in the win. The highlight of his night came in the first half, when he caught a pitch and burst loose for an 80-yard touchdown.

Tristan Sabb, Senior, Quarterback, DeMatha

Sabb shook off last week’s loss to WCAC rival St. John’s with a sterling performance on the road against Gonzaga on Saturday afternoon. The senior quarterback threw for two touchdowns and ran for another in the 30-14 victory, which helped the Stags secure a home game in the upcoming WCAC playoffs.

Sabb showed up when it mattered most — early in the fourth quarter, he jetted to the end zone for a rushing touchdown to give DeMatha a two-score advantage. The dagger came minutes later, when Sabb lofted a deep pass to senior wide receiver Austin Barber for a long score to put the game away.

Deyon Smith, Senior, Linebacker, Friendship Collegiate

Smith imposed his will on both sides of the ball for the Knights in a 30-18 win over Riverdale Baptist on Friday night. He was a dominant presence at middle linebacker for Friendship Collegiate, which held Riverdale Baptist to 18 points after the Crusaders averaged 42 in their three previous contests,

Smith racked up nine tackles in the win. He also rushed for 75 yards and punched in two touchdowns at running back for coach Mike Hunter’s team, now on a three-game winning streak heading into November.
entries.author: Noah Ferguson

entries.title: Abortion Opponents Warn Republicans That Ignoring the Issue Will Cost Them the Election
entries.summary: The president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America said not campaigning on abortion restrictions “could prove deadly for our prospects.”
entries.content:
Anti-abortion activists are lamenting a top-down campaign strategy that has largely ignored a motivating issue for much of the Republican base. Should the party have a bad showing on Election Day, a prominent group says President Donald Trump and other party leaders will be to blame for ignoring how an anti-abortion message could have aided Republicans.

“The power of the issue has not been prevailed upon by the party in general,” Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, told The Washington Sun, saying it was a failure at the top of the party. “It could prove deadly for our prospects.”

Activists have been raising concerns for months about the administration’s inaction on abortion restrictions — and those calls increased after The Sun reported that the White House was directing the Justice Department not to act on abortion — including not to act on abortion-related cases — until after the midterms. Republicans' campaign season has instead been defined by attempts to minimize political fallout from the Iran war, high gas prices and dissatisfaction with how the first two years of Trump’s second term have unfolded.

“The Trump Administration is committed to Gold Standard Science, as outlined in detail by President Trump’s Executive Order, ‘Restoring Gold Standard Science,’” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said in a statement to The Sun. “The mifepristone safety review by the FDA is just one example of President Trump's total commitment to ensuring the health and safety of all Americans.”

In outside ads and in Trump’s many red-state rallies, Republican candidates’ anti-abortion credentials have been left out of national messaging. Abortion opponents say the avoidance has sidelined a faction of single-issue voters.

While activists and faith groups have continued to focus on abortion restrictions as a motivator for the base and in local races and ballot measures, one Republican operative said the excitement about abortion access as a national issue only exists within Democratic circles.

“There’s a lot of enthusiasm on the left,” said the operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe party dynamics. “But I don’t see anybody talking about this from the GOP’s point of view.”

Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, defended Trump’s record on abortion, referring to him as “the most pro-life and pro-family president in American history.”

“Whether it’s ending the Biden DOJ’s weaponization of the FACE Act against peaceful protestors, expanding the child tax credit, creating Trump accounts, or making it easier to buy a home, there’s never been a president who cares more about our nation’s children and working families,” Baldassarre said in a statement to The Sun.

Conservatives worry that the de-emphasis on abortion will dampen turnout among evangelical voters. Dannenfelser said the effect could be more widespread, extending beyond evangelicals and into a larger bucket of voters who oppose abortion, including socially conservative Catholics who have become reliable Republican allies.

“The intensity killer is when there’s confusion or there’s a lack of leadership generally, and so it’s discouraging if it’s a qualifier for you,” Dannenfelser said. “It could be high impact in terms of voter intensity and a dearth of voters that are needed at the polls.”

In lieu of help from the outside groups central to the money boosting Republican candidates, Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America and other organizations have done their own outreach. SBA and its super PAC, Women Speak Out PAC, said they had logged roughly 3.34 million door-to-door voter visits from 2,315 canvassers as of last week. The group’s outreach also included over 19 million text messages and mailers.

Dannenfelser said SBA has done its part. If Republicans lose big on Tuesday, she predicted that those who cast aside abortion as a priority issue will be to blame.

“It really is a measurable difference that Democrats have figured is there,” she said. “They’re going to take advantage of it when they see it in battlegrounds, and we have to make up for it in all these races. So the question is whether we’ll be able to do it or not.”

Democrats have taken notice. As many Republican candidates have gone quiet about their positions on abortion, Democratic candidates in competitive states are spending the home stretch keen to discuss their opponents’ records on abortion.

“We know that they are worried about this issue and MAGA is scared,” Mini Timmaraju, president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, told reporters Thursday. “Republicans can see the writing on the wall.”

Polling conducted by RFA over the summer identified abortion as a swing issue. Poll participants didn’t prioritize it over affordability, but the group argues opposition to abortion can be a disqualifier in races where candidates share similar, populist economic messages.

“That’s why you’re seeing, here in the last three weeks, these Democratic candidates in these key congressional districts just running really hard on abortion,” said Alejandro Garcia, an RFA spokesperson.

In tight races, particularly in traditional swing districts and states, Democratic candidates have been loath to allow Republicans to distance themselves from the party’s traditional anti-abortion stance. Ads and mailers in Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire, among others, seek to tie Republican candidates to anti-abortion records.

RFA is spending $200,000 in digital ads to support Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s Senate seat, that they say will highlight Republican nominee Mike Rogers’ anti-abortion stances.

“In many of our competitive districts across the country, the issue of reproductive health has been a defining contrast,” said Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-Washington), chair of the House Democrats’ campaign arm. She said Democratic candidates are being vocal about preserving access to abortion “while Republicans are scrambling to hide their extreme views on the issue.”

Some anti-abortion activists say that conservative voters focused on policies that restrict abortion access won’t be tempted to stay home because local candidates have campaigned on the issue, even if it has been absent from the national conversation.

Suzi Voyles, an activist based in Georgia, said the state’s Republican candidates have distinguished themselves as anti-abortion.

“Everybody running here in Georgia, who is running as a Republican, is very pro-life,” Voyles said. “They have been very clear.”

Should Republicans prevail on Tuesday, Dannenfelser said, it would be an “unbelievable success story” against the political current. If they don’t, she said, the party needs to take it as a lesson.

“You better not leave your base behind,” she said. “It’s the fundamental political law of the land.”

entries.title: Spirit Beat Chicago, 2-0, Earn No. 3 Seed in NWSL Playoffs
entries.summary: Washington will host the Portland Thorns next Sunday in the first round of the postseason.
entries.content:
The Spirit’s first-round playoff matchup is set.

Washington will host the Portland Thorns at 3 p.m. next Sunday, after concluding the regular season with a 2-0 home win over the Chicago Stars.

The Spirit (17-9-4) earned the No. 3 seed in the NWSL playoff bracket. Portland is the No. 6 seed.

Trinity Rodman scored in the 85th minute to seal the win for the Spirit over the previously eliminated Stars (5-23-2) at Audi Field.

Rodman finished a pass from Clara Luvanga after being left unguarded in the penalty area. An own goal by Stars defender Michelle Alozie gave the Spirit the lead in the 62nd minute.

You can view the full NWSL playoff bracket here. Check back this week for more coverage leading into the Spirit's postseason opener.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Washington’s Much-Maligned Defense Just Helped Rescue Its Season
entries.summary: The Commanders' bye week featured plenty of palace intrigue and questions about the defensive coaching staff. But they played their best game against the Eagles.
entries.content:
You fought through your post-Halloween hangover, delighting in your extra hour of sleep — until it got dark before dinnertime, and you realized how interminable the wait would feel until the kickoff of "Sunday Night Football." You nonetheless made it to the Washington Commanders’ primetime game against the Philadelphia Eagles, where you expected to see a clean, redemptive performance befitting a home team coming off its bye week, against a bedraggled opponent that hadn’t won a game since mid-September.

This, decidedly, was not that.

But if the Commanders, with their season teetering and their embattled head coach looking increasingly vulnerable, had any hope of playing meaningful games in December and January, they had to win at Northwest Stadium on the first day of November.

Their 27-10 victory over the moribund Eagles wasn’t always easy on the eyes — with the offense still too prone to senseless penalties and red-zone failures. But it did feature the most complete performance of the season by their defense at a time when that unit was under intense scrutiny and palace intrigue.

Facing an Eagles offense decimated by injuries, the Commanders defense sacked fill-in quarterback Tanner McKee (starting in place of Jalen Hurts) five times and held perennial nemesis Saquon Barkley to just 30 yards on 13 carries. It forced a pair of turnovers and pitched a shutout across the final three quarters, allowing the offense the time and space to reel off 27 unanswered points.

“We heard all the noise that we weren’t getting sacks,” said veteran edge rusher Odafe Oweh, who had one of Washington’s five sacks. “So we applied that to our preparation. And we were blessed to be able to come out and not only be able to dominate on the D-line, the pass-rush and [against] the run, but also get the W. Wins fix everything.”

No one should read too much into a sometimes sloppy win against an Eagles team that featured a staggering 25 names on its mid-week injury report. But the victory, the first with Jayden Daniels at quarterback in nearly 13 months, nonetheless pushed the Commanders to 2-4-1, two games behind the first-place New York Giants in the NFC East, with the easiest stretch of their schedule on the horizon.

“We needed it,” said veteran safety Jeremy Reaves. “It’s about playing 60 [minutes]. That was the whole message [this week]. We’ve been good at stints of 15 or 30. But putting it all together — I’m just glad we did that tonight.”

The Eagles are two years removed from a Super Bowl championship and one year removed from a second consecutive NFC East title. The Commanders were two years removed from a trip to the NFC Championship Game. And yet one of them would see their 2026 season all but finished with a loss Sunday night, and even the winner would have to squint to see true playoff contention. It was, in other words, not an ideal matchup for the primetime slot on "Sunday Night Football."

Speculation about Dan Quinn’s status as the Commanders’ head coach has been building since the clock-management fiasco at the end of the Oct. 11 tie game at Northwest Stadium against the Giants, which cost the Commanders an all-but-certain last-second victory. And it was only somewhat muted by the second-half comeback at San Francisco that fell just short in Week 6, which led the Commanders, mercifully, into their bye week.

The 13-day gap between games did little to quiet the intrigue surrounding the Commanders, much of it focusing on the defense. The team managed to lose another key player, defensive tackle Daron Payne to a broken foot, despite not playing a game since Oct. 19.

But the more significant saga involved the coaching staff. First, the team brought on former Arizona Cardinals head coach Steve Wilks as a defensive consultant, saying the move had been planned since the start of the season but was only implemented in midseason.

Initially, the team indicated Wilks would work with the unit only in early-week practices, but not be part of the game-day staff. Days later, however, it was revealed that Wilks, a popular figure among players, would in fact be on the sideline Sunday night assisting defensive coordinator Daronte Jones — with whom he shares a background as a defensive backs coach — and possibly for additional games.

The team described the Wilks hiring as an additional resource for Jones, and Jones himself said he welcomed it. But the lack of clarity on the part of the team’s brain trust about the specifics of the move left all sorts of room for interpretation, which was soon filled by speculation and gossip. Was Wilks the new heir apparent in the event Quinn was fired? Was he there because Jones was seen as faltering in his first year as a coordinator?

It may have been a mere coincidence, but the Commanders’ best defensive effort of the season came in its first game with Wilks on the sideline.

Asked Sunday night what was different about what that defense was able to do against the Eagles that had been missing all season, Oweh replied, “We just did a good job of communicating.”

It was an interesting answer, given something Oweh said last week, when he told reporter Ben Standig that there had been some “miscommunication” between Jones and the team’s defensive position coaches (most of whom were holdovers from 2025, as opposed to Jones’ own hires). According to Oweh, sometimes those position coaches “didn’t understand the way Daronte saw it.” The implication was that the position coaches were having a hard time implementing Jones’ extremely blitz-heavy scheme within their individual position groups.

From “miscommunication” to “a good job of communicating,” something indeed changed for the Commanders on Sunday night. And while it’s too early to say it saved the team’s season, at the very least it kept it alive for another week.
entries.author: Dave Sheinin

entries.title: PAC Founder Won’t Press Charges After Ex-Treasurer Returns Money
entries.summary: Clifford Michael Pickens repaid more than $7,400 to the Existentialist Republic PAC, which is now shutting down.
entries.content:
The founder of the Existentialist Republic PAC told federal campaign finance regulators that he would not press charges against his former treasurer — and longtime friend — amid accusations of theft and misappropriation.

PAC founder Chris Armitage accused Clifford Michael Pickens in June of taking thousands of dollars from the political committee without approval — then disappearing. Armitage also said he was considering pressing charges against Pickens, who had been his friend for more than a decade.

But Pickens repaid the committee “in full,” Armitage told the Federal Election Commission on Saturday. Pickens repaid $3,500 on June 9 and the remaining $3,938 on June 15. Pickens also paid $61.26 as reimbursement for filing fees.

“After Mr. Pickens repaid in full, the committee did not pursue the complaints or the civil action described in its June 2” letter to the FEC, Armitage wrote.

The Existentialist Republic PAC then returned the money it had raised to the donors, according to Armitage. It has also filed paperwork to shut down its operations.

Upon its formation earlier this year, the Existentialist Republic PAC said it aimed to fund, organize and elect leaders “who believe in evidence-driven action and accountability.”

Pickens told The Washington Sun in June that he was "surprised" by Armitage’s accusations. He acknowledged he had “ignored a lot of people in my life” during a turbulent period in his personal life.

Armitage said he had contacted Pickens multiple times to inquire about the missing funds and couldn’t understand why his friend didn’t just talk to him.

Neither Armitage nor Pickens immediately responded to questions from The Sun, including about the status of their friendship.

Over the last decade, there have been countless allegations of once-trusted treasurers taking money from political campaigns and committees. In the last year alone, several have admitted to or been accused of stealing from trade associations, unions and political campaigns.
entries.author: Taylor Giorno
